extracted.intended_audience: students, coaches, team leaders, and general readers seeking IMO rules, format, and history
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of the International Mathematical Olympiad's contest format, eligibility, problem selection, scoring, awards, and disciplinary rules — intended to capture the standards by which problems, participants, and results are governed and evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition format and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest takes place over two consecutive days and consists of six problems (three given on each day). Each day, the contestants have four-and-a-half hours to solve three problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each problem session is 4.5 hours for three problems; the structure (two days, three problems/day) is fixed and determines pacing and time-management strategies for contestants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring per problem and total score
rubrics_metrics.description: Each problem is worth 7 points for a maximum total score of 42 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contestants' individual scores are out of 42; graders award up to 7 points per problem. Strategies that net full points on single problems (e.g., complete elegant solutions) are rewarded; partial-credit norms depend on coordinators/jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculators and measuring tools ban
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculators are banned. Protractors were banned relatively recently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No calculators (and no protractors) are allowed during the contest; bringing forbidden tools has led to penalties in the past (e.g., zero on a paper, disqualification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem topics and absence of official syllabus
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike other science olympiads, the IMO has no official syllabus and does not cover any university-level topics. The problems chosen are from various areas of secondary school mathematics, broadly classifiable as geometry, number theory, algebra, and combinatorics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems may include topics not conventionally covered in school but avoid the use of calculus; the contest favors elementary (though often disguised) methods and creativity rather than university-level material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle about calculus and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculus, though allowed in solutions, is never required, as there is a principle that anyone with a basic understanding of mathematics should understand the problems, even if the solutions require a great deal more knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem designers aim for universality and deceptively simple statements whose solutions demand ingenuity; use of higher math is discouraged as necessary apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common problem characteristics and emphases
rubrics_metrics.description: The problems are extremely difficult and may include topics not conventionally covered in school; the prominently featured problems are algebraic inequalities, complex numbers, and construction-oriented geometrical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In recent years certain techniques (e.g., Muirhead, complex/analytic bashing) have affected problem popularity; problem authors favor creativity, elegance, and challenge over routine application of advanced theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem submission and shortlisting
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participating country, other than the host country, may submit suggested problems to a problem selection committee provided by the host country, which reduces the submitted problems to a shortlist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National problem-submission is the primary source of candidate problems; hosts manage an initial filtering/shortlist before the jury selects final problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury selection of the six problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Team leaders arrive a few days in advance of the contestants and form the IMO jury, which is responsible for all the formal decisions relating to the contest, starting with selecting the six problems from the shortlist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury (composed of team leaders) has final say on the six problems and other formal contest decisions; leaders are kept strictly separated from contestants once problems are distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired ordering of problem difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury aims to order the problems so that the order in increasing difficulty is Q1, Q4, Q2, Q5, Q3, and Q6, where the first day problems Q1, Q2, and Q3 are in increasing difficulty, and the second day problems Q4, Q5, and Q6 are in increasing difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem ordering convention is intended to distribute difficulty across days and positions; actual perceived difficulty may vary and the jury attempts to respect this ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team composition and delegation roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Each country sends a team of up to six students, plus one team leader, one deputy leader, and observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams are nationally selected and accompanied by official leaders/deputies who participate in coordination, grading agreement, and the jury; team size limits shape national selection processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant eligibility (age and enrollment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contestants must be under the age of 20 and must not be registered at any tertiary institution. Subject to these conditions, an individual may participate any number of times in the IMO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility is strictly enforced; countries must verify age and enrollment status. No cap on number of participations provided age/enrollment criteria remain satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: National team selection variability
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection process differs by country, but it often consists of a series of tests that admit fewer students at each test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different countries use varied pipelines (e.g., camps in China, AMC/AIME/USAMO progression in the U.S., multi-year early selection in some former Soviet countries); selection methods affect training and preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medal awarding principle and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards are given to approximately the top-scoring 50% of the individual contestants. The cutoffs (minimum scores required to receive a gold, silver, or bronze medal respectively) are then chosen so that the numbers of gold, silver and bronze medals awarded are approximately in the ratios 1:2:3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medal cutoffs are set post-competition to yield target proportions; approximate rules govern allocation rather than fixed score thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorable mentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants who do not win a medal but who score 7 points on at least one problem receive an honorable mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving a full score on a single problem merits recognition even if overall medal thresholds are not met; this is an established convention for acknowledging outstanding single-problem work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special prizes criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Special prizes may be awarded for solutions of outstanding elegance or involving good generalisations of a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such prizes are rare and given at jury discretion to highlight exemplary solutions (examples cited: 1995 and 2005 winners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Team recognition and unofficial team scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams are not officially recognized—all scores are given only to individual contestants, but team scoring is unofficially compared more than individual scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although medals are individual, aggregate team performance is tracked and compared unofficially; official documentation focuses on individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark agreement and coordination process
rubrics_metrics.description: Each country's marks are agreed between that country's leader and deputy leader, and coordinators provided by the host country (the leader of the team whose country submitted the problem in the case of the marks of the host country), subject to the decisions of the chief coordinator and, ultimately, a jury if any disputes cannot be resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grading involves bilateral agreement (leader/deputy with host coordinators) and hierarchical dispute resolution up to the chief coordinator and jury; this process governs how points are assigned and disputes adjudicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary rules, penalties and historical precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: There have been cases of cheating and penalties, including disqualification (North Korea) and other penalties like zero scores for bringing forbidden items. Russia has been banned from participating since 2022 with limited exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict conduct and material rules are enforced; past incidents show a range of sanctions from zero points to disqualification or country bans. Political/sanction actions (e.g., bans) can affect participation and scoring inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception handling for medal proportion rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that at most half the contestants win a medal is sometimes broken if it would cause the total number of medals to deviate too much from half the number of contestants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In edge cases the jury/organizers may award slightly more than half medals to keep counts reasonable; historical examples: 2010, 2012, 2013 where >50% medals were awarded.
